svg.text: The database is a non-entity architecturally: a detail, like a doorknob to the architecture of a house. Not the data model (the structure of data in the application is
highly significant); the database is a utility, a mechanism, that provides access to the data
Relational databases
Edgar Codd defined the principles in 1970; dominant by the mid-1980s: elegant,
disciplined, robust; yet a technology, so a detail. Use cases should not know the
tabular structure; passing rows and tables around as objects couples use cases,
business rules and sometimes the UI to the relational structure: an architectural
error
Why databases are prevalent: disks
rotating magnetic disks were the mainstay for five decades: 48-inch platters
holding 20 megabytes to a few-gram 3-inch disk holding a terabyte, always slow (a
millisecond is a million times a processor cycle): so indexes, caches, optimised
queries, and two kinds of systems: file systems (document based) and RDBMS (content
based)
What if there were no disk?
disks are a dying breed, replaced by RAM; you would organise data as linked lists,
trees, hash tables, stacks and queues accessed by references, not tables and SQL;
indeed you already reorganise data loaded from a database into such structures
Details and performance
the database is a bucket of bits moving data between disk and RAM; we should not
even acknowledge the disk; performance is an architectural concern, but for storage
it is fully encapsulated and separate from business rules: a low-level data access
matter
Anecdote (late 1980s, T1 line network management): random access files with trees and linked lists were enough, but marketing, and a hardware engineer who became
software manager, insisted on an RDBMS because customers expected it (a check-box item from vendor marketing); Martin was right on engineering, wrong on the market; he
should have bolted an RDBMS on the side behind a narrow, safe channel. The data model is significant; the database is a detail.
